article_title: Enabling Multi-Agent Systems as Learning Designers: Applying Learning Sciences to AI Instructional Design
citation: Jiayi Wang, Ruiwei Xiao, Xinying Hou, John Stamper. (2025). Enabling Multi-Agent Systems as Learning Designers: Applying Learning Sciences to AI Instructional Design. https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.16659
title: Knowledge–Learning–Instruction (KLI) framework as an organizing theory for AI instructional design
description: The KLI framework connects knowledge components, learning processes, and instructional principles to support robust learning. The article states that "effective instruction requires careful alignment among three core elements": Knowledge Components as the goals of learning, Learning Processes describing how learning occurs, and Instructional Principles as the methods facilitating those processes. The authors use KLI to guide the reasoning of their multi-agent systems, grounding AI instructional design in an evidence-based instructional theory rather than leaving pedagogy to user prompts.
requirements: The system must map subject domain, grade level, standard alignment, and learning objectives into knowledge components, then select learning processes and instructional principles before activity generation
constraints: The study was limited to a single pedagogical framework (KLI) and a specific set of MAS architectures
target_learners: K-12 secondary mathematics and science students
target_learning_goals: Curriculum-aligned STEM learning objectives from authentic lesson plan libraries
examples: The MAS-Roles system operationalizes KLI through a five-stage pipeline of KC, Learning Process, Instructional Principle, Design, and Feedback agents; MAS-CMD gives all three persona agents the same KLI guidance
key_sources: Jiayi Wang, Ruiwei Xiao, Xinying Hou, John Stamper. (2025). Enabling Multi-Agent Systems as Learning Designers: Applying Learning Sciences to AI Instructional Design. https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.16659

article_title: Evidence and Theory for why the Best Example-Problem Ratio To Optimize Learning Gain Depends on Knowledge Content
citation: Rachatasumrit, N., Koedinger, K. R., & Carvalho, P. F. (2023). Evidence and theory for why the best example-problem ratio to optimize learning gain depends on knowledge content. https://osf.io/29wpe
title: Knowledge-Learning-Instruction (KLI) framework: knowledge-component taxonomy linking content type to learning processes and instructional principles
description: The KLI framework is a taxonomic and conceptual framework relating instructional events, learning events, and knowledge components (KCs). It classifies KCs by whether conditions and responses are constant or variable: verbatim facts are constant-condition, constant-response KCs, while skills such as computing a shape's area are variable-condition, variable-response KCs. The article uses KLI to predict that memory and fluency processes suit facts whereas induction and refinement processes suit skills, explaining why retrieval practice benefits facts and example study benefits skills.
requirements: A clear classification of knowledge content, as the article states testing the hypothesis requires
constraints: Learning events and knowledge components cannot be directly observed and must be inferred from assessment events
target_learners: K-12 and adult learners acquiring facts and skills
examples: The article classifies 'Sudan has the most pyramids of any country in the world' as a constant-condition, constant-response KC and triangle-area calculation as a variable-condition, variable-response KC
key_sources: Rachatasumrit, N., Koedinger, K. R., & Carvalho, P. F. (2023). Evidence and theory for why the best example-problem ratio to optimize learning gain depends on knowledge content. https://osf.io/29wpe

article_title: The knowledge-learning-instruction (KLI) framework: Toward bridging the science-practice chasm to enhance robust student learning
citation: Kenneth R. Koedinger, Albert T. Corbett, Charles Perfetti. (2010). The Knowledge-Learning-Instruction (KLI) Framework: Toward Bridging the Science-Practice Chasm to Enhance Robust Student Learning. Carnegie Mellon University Technical Report. http://learnlab.org/research/wiki
title: The Knowledge-Learning-Instruction (KLI) Framework: an intermediate-grain-size framework linking knowledge components, learning events and instructional events
description: The KLI Framework is a theoretical framework (not a falsifiable theory) with three components: a taxonomy of knowledge components, learning processes, and instructional principles. It targets an intermediate 'learning event' grain size between neural theories and macro-level educational theories, so that propositions are 'empirical claims, so they are testable by experiments' and translate both downward to mechanisms and upward to instruction. Its scope is conditions yielding robust learning: long-term retention, transfer, and accelerated future learning.
requirements: Propositions must be elaborated with added assumptions to become theories that generate falsifiable predictions
constraints: The framework itself does not generate precise, falsifiable predictions at the level of theory
Generalizations carry grade- or experience-level boundary conditions from middle school, high school, and early college settings
target_learners: middle school, high school, and early college students in academic courses
target_learning_goals: robust student learning: long-term retention, transfer, and accelerated future learning across academic domains
examples: The framework is grounded in PSLC LearnLab courses spanning Physics, Chemistry, Algebra, Geometry, French, Chinese, and English as a second language
key_sources: Kenneth R. Koedinger, Albert T. Corbett, Charles Perfetti. (2010). The Knowledge-Learning-Instruction (KLI) Framework: Toward Bridging the Science-Practice Chasm to Enhance Robust Student Learning. Carnegie Mellon University Technical Report. http://learnlab.org/research/wiki

article_title: The knowledge-learning-instruction (KLI) framework: Toward bridging the science-practice chasm to enhance robust student learning
citation: Kenneth R. Koedinger, Albert T. Corbett, Charles Perfetti. (2010). The Knowledge-Learning-Instruction (KLI) Framework: Toward Bridging the Science-Practice Chasm to Enhance Robust Student Learning. Carnegie Mellon University Technical Report. http://learnlab.org/research/wiki
title: Taxonomy of knowledge components classified by task features, response, relationship, and rationale
description: The article defines a knowledge component as 'an acquired unit of cognitive function or structure that can be inferred from performance on a set of related tasks' and classifies KCs along four dimensions: whether task features and response are constant or variable, whether the feature-response relationship is implicit or explicit, and whether a rationale is known. This yields categories such as facts (constant-constant, explicit), categories and concepts (variable-constant), productions, skills, rules and plans (variable-variable), and principles with rationales. KCs are chosen at the level where novice students actually make errors.
requirements: KC analysis should stop unpacking when smaller components are performed with sufficiently high accuracy and fluency
KCs must be empirically derived from performance on assessment events rather than pre-determined by designers
constraints: Labels are rough mappings and not necessarily one-to-one with taxonomy cells; the authors note it is an open question whether all 16 cells of the 4-dimensional space exist
target_learners: students in second language, mathematics, and science courses
target_learning_goals: analyzing learning goals into knowledge components to guide instructional design and predict learning difficulty
examples: Table 2 gives examples such as the Chinese radical 日 mapping to 'sun' (a fact), English article selection (a category), and forming plurals (a rule)
key_sources: Kenneth R. Koedinger, Albert T. Corbett, Charles Perfetti. (2010). The Knowledge-Learning-Instruction (KLI) Framework: Toward Bridging the Science-Practice Chasm to Enhance Robust Student Learning. Carnegie Mellon University Technical Report. http://learnlab.org/research/wiki

article_title: What Video Games Have Taught Us: Two Decades of Gaming and Learning
citation: Kirk M. Lundblade. (2025). What Video Games Have Taught Us: Two Decades of Gaming and Learning. In Historiographies of Game Studies (Punctum Books). https://www.jstor.org/stable/jj.31913371.9
title: Klein's typology of interdisciplinarity by scope and subtype
description: The chapter borrows Julie Thompson Klein's grammar for assessing interdisciplinarity, stating: "we can assess interdisciplinarity in terms of scope — from narrow to broad — and in terms of subtype — methodological, theoretical, instrumental, or critical." The typology sits between multidisciplinarity, defined as juxtaposition of separate disciplinary inputs, and transdisciplinarity, which transcends disciplinary worldviews through overarching synthesis. The chapter uses it to classify Gee's work as instrumental multidisciplinarity.
requirements: Assessment requires examining how sources from another discipline are incorporated and for what purpose
constraints: Applied in the chapter to a single case study, Gee's monograph
target_learners: scholars and researchers studying interdisciplinary fields
target_learning_goals: understanding disciplinary boundary work and interdisciplinarity
examples: The chapter classifies Gee's 2007 revisions as instrumental multidisciplinarity under this typology
key_sources: Kirk M. Lundblade. (2025). What Video Games Have Taught Us: Two Decades of Gaming and Learning. In Historiographies of Game Studies (Punctum Books). https://www.jstor.org/stable/jj.31913371.9

article_title: Online Assessment and Game-Based Development of Inductive Reasoning
citation: Pásztor, Attila, Andrea Magyar, Anita Pásztor-Kovács, and Attila Rausch. 2022. Online Assessment and Game-Based Development of Inductive Reasoning. Journal of Intelligence 10: 59. https://doi.org/10.3390/jintelligence10030059
title: Klauer's model of inductive reasoning as six comparison-based processes
description: Klauer's theory defines inductive reasoning as detecting regularities and irregularities through comparison, crossed by two facets: whether similarity, difference, or both must be detected (facet A) and whether attributes or relations are involved (facet B), yielding six processes: Generalization, Discrimination, Cross classification, Recognizing relationships, Differentiating relationships, and System construction. The article states "the core process of inductive reasoning is comparison" and distinguishes inductive reasoning from inductive inference, which goes beyond the situation to unobserved cases. The study operationalized each process with specific item formats such as class formation, analogies, and matrices.
requirements: Assessment and training tasks must be designed per process, with item formats matched to the cognitive operation required (e.g., matrices for System construction)
constraints: The article notes a prior study (de Koning et al. 2003) found the construct unidimensional, and the 1-dimensional model's fit was also acceptable in this study
target_learners: fifth-grade students (model tested across ages in prior programs)
target_learning_goals: inductive reasoning: detecting regularities and irregularities in attributes and relations
examples: The online figurative test operationalized each process: class formation for Generalization, odd-one-out for Discrimination, 4-fold schemes for Cross classification, analogies for Recognizing relationships, disturbed series for Differentiating relationships, matrices for System construction
key_sources: Pásztor, Attila, Andrea Magyar, Anita Pásztor-Kovács, and Attila Rausch. 2022. Online Assessment and Game-Based Development of Inductive Reasoning. Journal of Intelligence 10: 59. https://doi.org/10.3390/jintelligence10030059

article_title: Problem-solving prior to instructional explanations when learning javelin throwing in primary school
citation: Christian Leukel, Katharina Loibl. (2025). Problem-solving prior to instructional explanations when learning javelin throwing in primary school. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09700-9
title: KLI framework for composite instructional designs: intermediate knowledge from the PS phase anchors processing of subsequent instruction
description: The article applies the knowledge-learning-instruction (KLI) framework, containing knowledge components, learning processes, and instructional design, as specified for composite instructional designs with two or more phases like PS-I. A key element is the intermediate knowledge after the first phase: knowledge activated during PS is incomplete and/or contains errors, but with the instructional explanation in the I phase it "can further evolve and be refined towards the target knowledge" and "serves as an anchor which supports the processing of the instructional explanations." The framework predicts PS-I benefits when declarative knowledge built during PS links to the content of I.
requirements: Students must generate intermediate knowledge during the PS phase that is pertinent to the content of the subsequent instructional explanations for integration to occur
constraints: The article reports that primary school children's limited ability to develop declarative knowledge during PS that links to the content of I may explain the absent PS-I advantage in this study
target_learners: primary school children (4th graders) learning motor skills in physical education
target_learning_goals: acquisition of complex motor skills such as javelin throwing, including execution of movement features
examples: The study applied the framework to javelin throwing, depicting the interplay of knowledge components, learning processes, and instructional design across PS and I phases (Fig. 1)
key_sources: Christian Leukel, Katharina Loibl. (2025). Problem-solving prior to instructional explanations when learning javelin throwing in primary school. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09700-9

article_title: Working memory capacity and disfluency effect: an aptitude-treatment-interaction study
citation: Janina Lehmann, Christina Goussios, Tina Seufert. (2015). Working memory capacity and disfluency effect: an aptitude-treatment-interaction study. Metacognition Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-015-9149-z
title: Differentiated subjective Cognitive Load Questionnaire measuring ICL, ECL and GCL
description: The study employed the paper-based Cognitive Load Questionnaire (Klepsch and Seufert 2012) to differentially assess the three types of cognitive load: three items each for intrinsic, extraneous, and germane load, rated on seven-point Likert scales after learning and after assessing learning outcomes. The authors note that "we were the first to use a differentiated measurement of the three types of CL in disfluency research". The instrument captures only subjective ratings of cognitive load, which the authors acknowledge may not coincide with objective load.
requirements: Learners must be aware of their own cognitive load for subjective ratings to be meaningful
constraints: Measures only subjectively perceived cognitive load, not objective load
Items may not cover all facets of ECL or subsemantic processes relevant to GCL
target_learners: University students learning from text-based material
target_learning_goals: Assessment of intrinsic, extraneous and germane cognitive load during learning
examples: Items included 'For this task many things needed to be kept in mind simultaneously.' for ICL and 'The design of this task was very inappropriate to really learn something.' for ECL
key_sources: Janina Lehmann, Christina Goussios, Tina Seufert. (2015). Working memory capacity and disfluency effect: an aptitude-treatment-interaction study. Metacognition Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-015-9149-z

article_title: Some experimental evidence in regard to formal discipline.
citation: Linus W. Kline, Ph.D. (1909). Some Experimental Evidence in Regard to Formal Discipline. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.google.com/search?q=%22Some+experimental+evidence+in+regard+to+formal+discipline%22+Kline
title: Attention-gateway account of transfer: mental life levies a tax on special processes through attention
description: The article offers an explanatory account of why practice transfers positively or negatively: attention directed to mere form in one task can prejudice performance on a task requiring meaning, and general mental functioning is affected through attention. The author writes, "It is as if our mental life, as a whole, levies a tax for general purposes upon special processes and that the manner and application of the levy are made through the gateway of attention." This interprets both studies' transfer asymmetries as changes in attitudes of attention rather than generic discipline of faculties.
requirements: Both the practiced and transfer tasks must be performed under conditions where attention can be directed to form versus meaning, as in the letter-versus-parts-of-speech tasks.
constraints: The account is the authors' interpretation of two small experiments, not a separately tested mechanism; the article cites Angell and Judd's symposium as its theoretical support.
target_learners: adult students in educational psychology courses
target_learning_goals: understanding how practice on one task affects performance on related tasks
examples: Subjects reported that e's and t's claimed attention even in irrelevant words, and the author noted the illusion persisted for six months.
key_sources: Linus W. Kline, Ph.D. (1909). Some Experimental Evidence in Regard to Formal Discipline. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.google.com/search?q=%22Some+experimental+evidence+in+regard+to+formal+discipline%22+Kline

article_title: Help Helps, But Only So Much: Research on Help Seeking with Intelligent Tutoring Systems
citation: Aleven, V., Roll, I., McLaren, B. M., & Koedinger, K. R. (2016). Help Helps, But Only So Much: Research on Help Seeking with Intelligent Tutoring Systems. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0089-1
title: KLI-based theoretical analysis: hints aid learning only when students make sense of them
description: The article uses the Knowledge-Learning-Instruction (KLI) framework to argue that a limited but non-negligible role exists for principle-based tutor hints. Under KLI, instruction must match the complexity of targeted knowledge: conceptual knowledge requires sense-making processes such as self-explanation, while procedural knowledge is best built through induction and refinement during problem-solving practice. "In short, the theoretical analysis suggests that help helps, but only so much." Hints may aid conceptual learning and may help procedural learning indirectly, for example by helping students identify relevant problem features. This analysis marks a shift from the authors' 2006 viewpoint by foregrounding the sense-making processes required for hints to work.
requirements: Students must self-explain the hints or otherwise make sense of them for the beneficial effects to occur
constraints: Takes a strong cognitive perspective without addressing social, motivational, and metacognitive aspects of help seeking, which could change the analysis
target_learners: Novice students learning complex domains such as geometry with step-based tutors
target_learning_goals: Conceptual knowledge of principles and procedural problem-solving skill
examples: The analysis predicts hints are not directly useful for acquiring procedural knowledge, since verbal sense making cannot influence non-verbal learning directly
key_sources: Aleven, V., Roll, I., McLaren, B. M., & Koedinger, K. R. (2016). Help Helps, But Only So Much: Research on Help Seeking with Intelligent Tutoring Systems. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0089-1
